International Law. The body of rules and treaties that govern relations between nation-states and define rights and obligations in war, trade, diplomacy, and shared domains like the ocean and space. Though ancient rulers made binding agreements, modern international law emerged from European treaties after the Thirty Years' War and evolved dramatically through the twentieth century. The League of Nations and United Nations institutionalized this framework, while concepts like war crimes and crimes against humanity have slowly been enforced. International law originates in the Peace of Westphalia in sixteen forty-eight, which established principles of state sovereignty and binding treaties between equals. Treaties are binding agreements that constitute the primary source of international law. Customary international law develops through consistent state practice. The League of Nations, established in nineteen twenty, was the first attempt to institutionalize international law, though it failed to prevent World War II. The United Nations, established in nineteen forty-five, replaced the League and established the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and other frameworks for peaceful resolution of disputes. War crimes and crimes against humanity emerged as legal categories after World War II, enforced through the Nuremberg Trials and subsequent tribunals. Modern challenges include enforcing international law against powerful nations, addressing cyber warfare and terrorism, and adjudicating disputes through the International Court of Justice. The Geneva Conventions codify rules protecting civilians, prisoners of war, and the wounded during armed conflict, establishing universal standards of conduct in war. Sovereignty and non-intervention are central principles, yet humanitarian intervention and responsibility to protect have emerged as counterbalancing doctrines justifying intervention to stop atrocities.
